question: Across the twelve months of 2025, did monthly cancellation rate and average Delivered-order delivery time move together? Report their monthly Pearson correlation, the number of months used, and whether that alone supports a causal claim.

action.query:
SELECT
  d.MONTH AS MONTH,
  SUM(CASE WHEN f.IS_CANCELLED THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS CANCELLED_ORDER_COUNT,
  COUNT(f.ORDER_ID) AS TOTAL_ORDER_COUNT,
  SUM(CASE WHEN f.IS_DELIVERED THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS DELIVERED_ORDER_COUNT,
  SUM(CASE WHEN f.IS_DELIVERED THEN f.DELIVERY_TIME_MIN ELSE 0 END) AS DELIVERED_DELIVERY_TIME_SUM_MIN
FROM ZOMATO_DLR.CORE.FACT_ORDER f
JOIN ZOMATO_DLR.CORE.DIM_DATE d ON f.ORDER_DATE = d.DATE_DAY
WHERE f.ORDER_DATE >= '2025-01-01' AND f.ORDER_DATE < '2026-01-01'
GROUP BY d.MONTH
ORDER BY d.MONTH;
action.metrics: monthly cancellation rate, monthly average delivered-order delivery time
Pearson correlation between monthly cancellation rate and average delivered-order delivery time; number of months used
action.answer: For each month in 2025, the cancellation rate was calculated as CANCELLED_ORDER_COUNT / TOTAL_ORDER_COUNT, and the average delivered-order delivery time as DELIVERED_DELIVERY_TIME_SUM_MIN / DELIVERED_ORDER_COUNT. Using the 12 monthly pairs, the Pearson correlation between cancellation rate and average delivered-order delivery time is approximately 0.997964. All 12 months were used. This very high positive correlation means that, in 2025, months with higher cancellation rates also tended to have higher average delivery times for delivered orders. However, correlation alone does not support a causal claim; other factors could drive both metrics, and further analysis would be needed to establish causality.
action.reason: All requested values are included: the correlation (0.997964), the number of months (12), and an interpretation. The answer notes that correlation does not prove causation.
